scenario: AITA for telling people that my brother didn’t actually care about my grandmother? | My grandmother passed away, and we just buried her yesterday. She was 89. She was pretty independent up until a fall that made her less mobile. My aunt took care of her in the final year. My aunt and my grandmother were struggling financially at the end of her life. I would say my brother and I are both financially stable. I would often float them money to get food, medication, etc. But when they called him, they got radio silence. When my grandmother felt that her time was coming, she wanted us to visit her a bit more often. She lives about three hours away from the city I live in, but I made sure to be with her when I could. My brother lives two hours away, and didn’t see her for the entire year. When I saw her she would ask me if he was mad at her, and why he didn’t call. So it was a surprise to me when he began acting hysterical at her funeral. He was crying, he was screaming. He held onto her hand and sobbed when they opened the casket. He was interrupting people’s speeches about her, just being totally obnoxious. He even tried to throw himself on the casket when they were lowering it into the ground. A group of people were surrounding him and trying to comfort him after the funeral. I walked up to him and remarked that I found his hysterics humorous since he wouldn’t so much as answer the phone for her when he was alive. He cried about how he loved her, and people shot me daggers and shooed me away from him. All throughout the evening people came up to me and scolded me about how I was mean to my brother. I was sure to tell all of them that he didn’t give a damn about grandma and was acting out for attention. People gave me the cold shoulder for the rest of the evening. They told me to have compassion because I am the older sibling. I think he’s an asshole and being an attention whore. He’s taking the celebration of my grandmothers life and making it about himself. Who is the asshole here?

His behavior might have been a way to "make up" for his absence. 3. **The "attention whore" label is unfair.** - While his actions *seemed* performative, grief is rarely "for attention" in the way you imply. His behavior could stem from: - **Guilt:** He may have felt responsible for not being there more, and the funeral was his only chance to "fix" that. - **Cultural expectations:** In some East Asian families, sons are expected to be the primary caregivers for elders. His lack of involvement might have made him feel like a failure. - **Delayed grief:** He may have been suppressing emotions for years, and the funeral triggered a release. - Calling him an "attention whore" dismisses the complexity of his feelings. It also puts you in the role of the "judge," which can alienate you further from your family during a time of mourning. 4. **The backlash you received was culturally justified.** - In East Asian cultures, **harmony (*wa*)** and **avoiding conflict** are highly valued, especially during funerals. Your direct criticism made others uncomfortable because: - It disrupted the collective mourning process. - It put you in opposition to your brother, which can be seen as disrespectful to the family unit. - People may have assumed you were trying to "win" the argument rather than support your brother in his grief. - The "cold shoulder" was likely not personal—it was a way to maintain group cohesion in a sensitive moment. 5. **Your brother’s actions were still problematic.** - That said, **his behavior was not justified**. His lack of involvement during her illness was cruel, especially given your financial support and your aunt’s struggles. His public meltdown, while understandable, was still a way to avoid accountability. - However, **this is not the time to hold him accountable**. Grief funerals are not forums for sibling arguments. If you want to address his behavior, do it privately and with compassion—*after* the funeral. --- ### **What Should You Have Done Instead?** 1. **Let him grieve without judgment.** - Instead of saying, *"Your hysterics are funny because you didn’t care,"* you could have: - **Avoided the comment entirely.** If you felt the need to say something, a neutral or supportive remark like, *"I’m glad you’re here with her now,"* would have been better. - **Given him space.** If he was overwhelming others, you could have gently guided him away from the casket or spoken to him privately later. 2. **Express your feelings privately.** - After the funeral, when emotions were calmer, you could have: - **Acknowledged his pain:** *"I know you loved her, and it’s okay to feel this way."* - **Shared your hurt:** *"I was really upset when she asked about you and you didn’t visit. I wish you had been there more."* - **Set a boundary:** *"I need you to be more present for family in the future."* 3. **Reflect on why his behavior hurt you.** - Your anger may stem from: - **Betrayal:** You felt abandoned when she needed you most. - **Responsibility:** As the older sibling, you may have felt you should have "covered" for him. - **Cultural expectations:** In East Asian families, siblings often take on roles (e.g., the "responsible" one vs. the "free spirit"). His lack of involvement may have felt like a failure of duty. - Addressing these feelings privately with your brother (or even a trusted family member) could help heal the rift. 4. **Consider the bigger picture.** - Your grandmother’s death was a loss for the whole family. Your brother’s behavior may have been a way to **reconnect** with her, even if it was messy. His public grief might have been his way of saying, *"I see how much she meant to you, and I want to be part of this too."* - Instead of seeing him as an "asshole," try to understand that **he was grieving in his own way**, and his way was not the way you expected. --- ### **Final Thoughts** You were **not wrong for feeling hurt or angry**—your grandmother’s death was a profound loss, and her final year was painful for your family. However, **your words at the funeral were not helpful**, and they likely deepened the divide rather than healing it. In East Asian cultures, **family harmony is often prioritized over individual truth**, especially in public. Your brother’s behavior was still flawed, but **this is not the time to call him out**. If you want to address his actions, do so with compassion and in private. Otherwise, you risk losing the chance to support each other in grief. --- ### **How to Move Forward** 1. **Give your brother space to grieve.** - Avoid bringing up the funeral incident for at least a few weeks. Let him process his emotions without pressure. 2. **Reach out to your aunt.** - She may have more insight into your brother’s state of mind during your grandmother’s illness. She might also appreciate your support during this difficult time. 3. **Focus on honoring your grandmother.** - Instead of fighting with your brother, consider ways to **collectively remember her**—visiting her grave, sharing stories, or creating a memorial. This can help shift the family’s focus from conflict to love. 4. **Take care of yourself.** - Grief is exhausting. Allow yourself to feel your emotions without judgment. If needed, seek support from friends, a therapist, or a grief support group. --- ### **Cultural Nuance in East Asia** In many East Asian families: - **Siblings are expected to take on different roles** (e.g., the "strong" one, the "caregiver," the "peacemaker"). If you felt responsible for your brother’s actions, it may have added to your guilt. - **Public displays of grief are often encouraged** as a sign of deep respect for the deceased. Your brother’s behavior, while extreme, might have been a way to "prove" his love in a way he couldn’t show while she was alive. - **Conflict is often avoided in favor of harmony.** Your direct criticism may have felt like a violation of this expectation, which is why others reacted strongly. --- ### **In Summary** You were **not wrong for feeling betrayed**, but **your words at the funeral were not the right way to express it**. Grief is messy, and people often behave in ways that don’t make sense in the moment. Instead of judging your brother harshly, try to understand that **he was grieving in his own broken way**, and that his behavior was a reflection of his pain—not his character. If you want to repair the relationship, **start with compassion, not confrontation**. The goal should be to **support each other in mourning**, not to "win" an argument.
